title: Let It Become Real
author: Kathleen Schafer
summary: Kathleen Schafer writes to the exhaustion of change agents who have been measuring their impact by spectacle -- by the size of the audience, the reach of the platform, the impressiveness of the initiative -- rather than by whether what they know to be true is actually embodied in how they show up in the ordinary moments of community life. The article's intellectual anchor is Buckminster Fuller's trim tab metaphor: a tiny rudder that turns the main rudder that turns the ship, where the leverage is not size but placement within the system. Schafer argues that transformation moves through people who are already embedded in a community with credibility and trust -- not through the most credentialed outsider or the largest platform -- and that the work of those embedded people is not to perform transformation but to let what is true about what they believe become visible in one grounded act at a time. The invitation is explicit and counter-cultural in an attention-economy context: stop auditing impact through metrics of reach and start asking whether the thing you believe is actually becoming real in the relationships and decisions closest to you. Small grounded acts compound over time; the compounding is slow and invisible until it is not. The closing section frames this as a form of integrity rather than a strategy: the question is not 'What is the most effective thing I can do?' but 'Am I letting what I believe become real?'
points: The trim tab principle reframes where leverage lives: not in scale or credential but in placement -- the person already embedded in a community with existing trust is the one whose small act turns the larger system.

Measuring impact by spectacle -- platform reach, initiative size, audience metrics -- is a form of self-deception that substitutes external validation for the harder question of whether beliefs are actually embodied in practice.
Transformation moves through embedded community members with accumulated relational credibility, not through credentialed outsiders deploying expertise at scale.
Small grounded acts compound in ways that are invisible until they are not; the impatience to see large effects quickly is what causes change agents to abandon the leverage they already have.
The question is not strategic -- 'What is the most effective thing I can do?' -- but integrous: 'Is what I believe actually becoming real in the relationships and decisions closest to me?'
quotes: We are exhausted by the performance of change. The keynote, the initiative, the launch. And then the quiet moment when we wonder if any of it moved anything at all.

Fuller called it the trim tab. A small rudder that turns the main rudder that turns the ship. The leverage is not in the size. It is in where you are placed in the system, and whether you are willing to move.

Transformation does not travel through the most credentialed or the most visible. It travels through the person already in the room -- already trusted, already embedded -- who decides to let what they know become visible in how they act.
Stop counting reach. Start asking whether the thing you believe is becoming real -- in the meeting, in the conversation, in the decision you made last Tuesday when no one was watching.
This is not a strategy. It is an integrity question. Am I letting what I believe become real? One grounded act at a time, in the places I actually inhabit. That is the work.
